entities.summary:
Iphicrates, an innovative Athenian general operating primarily between 390 and 370 BCE, profoundly reshaped ancient Greek infantry tactics through his pioneering reforms of the peltast corps. Operating amidst the shifting power dynamics of the Corinthian War and subsequent conflicts, his military innovations challenged the long-dominant hoplite phalanx and introduced a more flexible, light-armed fighting style, directly influencing the professionalization of Hellenic armies and laying groundwork for later Macedonian military developments. His career unfolded against the backdrop of Sparta's waning hegemony and Thebes's brief ascendancy, positioning Athens to reclaim a measure of its former military prestige.

Iphicrates's most famous achievement occurred in 390 BCE during the Corinthian War when his peltasts annihilated a Spartan mora (a unit of 500-600 hoplites) near Lechaeum. This victory, described by Xenophon, demonstrated the decisive superiority of his re-equipped and rigorously trained light infantry over traditional heavy infantry on broken terrain. His reforms involved extending the spear (dory) and sword, replacing heavy greaves and shields (hoplon) with lighter equivalents, and emphasizing skirmishing and rapid maneuver over static line engagements. Beyond Lechaeum, Iphicrates also commanded Athenian forces in Thrace, against the Persian satrap Pharnabazus, and in Egypt, showcasing his adaptability across various theaters.
